answer_text:
Assume the standard (non-induced) extremal number: \(\operatorname{ex}(n;P)\) is the maximum number of edges in an \(n\)-vertex graph with no subgraph isomorphic to the Petersen graph \(P\).

1. **Chromatic number of the Petersen graph.**  
   The Petersen graph contains a \(5\)-cycle, so it is not bipartite:
   \[
   \chi(P)\ge 3.
   \]
   It is 3-colorable. For example, with the usual labeling by outer vertices \(u_i\) and inner vertices \(v_i\), \(i=0,\dots,4\), with edges
   \[
   u_iu_{i+1},\quad u_iv_i,\quad v_iv_{i+2}\pmod 5,
   \]
   a proper 3-coloring is
   \[
   u_i: 1,2,3,1,2,\qquad v_i: 2,1,1,3,3.
   \]
   Hence
   \[
   \chi(P)=3.
   \]

2. **Apply the Erdős–Stone–Simonovits theorem.**  
   For any fixed graph \(F\) with chromatic number \(r\),
   \[
   \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{ex}(n;F)}{\binom n2}
   =1-\frac1{r-1}.
   \]
   Since \(r=\chi(P)=3\), we get
   \[
   \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{\operatorname{ex}(n;P)}{\binom n2}
   =1-\frac12=\frac12.
   \]

Equivalently, \(\operatorname{ex}(n;P)=\frac14 n^2+o(n^2)\), while \(\binom n2=\frac12 n^2+O(n)\), so the ratio tends to \(\frac12\).

\[
\boxed{\frac12}
\]
